meta.title: Slidemaster Framework
meta.subtitle: From a raw idea to a rehearsed talk
meta.author: Johan Wallquist
meta.audience: Presenters who prepare talks and workshops with an AI assistant
meta.centralClaim: A talk gets better when the thinking happens before the slides, and an AI assistant can run that process with you.
meta.audienceAction: Talk about the idea for your next talk, out loud and unedited, then let your assistant take it through the six stages.

content.heading: The slides are the easy part
content.lead: Slidemaster takes a talk from a raw idea to a rehearsed presentation. An AI assistant does the legwork. You keep the words.

notes.do: Let the title sit. Pause before you speak.
notes.say: Ask any assistant for a deck and you have one in a minute. Headings and bullets, maybe an icon, and it already looks finished. But that's the easy part. You still have to decide what you want to test and whether the proof holds up, then fit the talk into the minutes you've got and practice it. That's the work I built this framework for, starting with my own keynotes. In the next fifteen minutes I'll show you how it works, so you can try it on your next talk.

content.heading: Most decks start in the wrong place
content.lead: Open a slide tool, or ask an assistant for slides.

data.text: You get a layout before you have a point.

notes.do: Ask who opened a deck before they knew their point. Wait for hands.
notes.say: Someone books you for a talk, and the same afternoon you're filling in a deck. Title slide and agenda, then the boxes. We've all done it. With an assistant the boxes fill themselves, before you've decided what you actually want to say. Generic claims. No sources, and nobody pushing back. But there's a deck to work on, so you keep going. Nobody adds up the minutes until the first run-through, usually the night before. The layout was never the problem. The order was.

content.heading: It started with my own keynotes

data.text: The method worked. But every new talk began by copying the last one.

notes.do: Slow down. Tell it as a story.
notes.say: This autumn I prepared two keynotes with an AI assistant. Both started with me talking about the idea, out loud and unedited, and the assistant pulling out the claims, so we could research each one and find its strongest counterargument. Before any slides, I went through my old decks for things to reuse and worked out the minutes. Then came the outline. We rewrote it over and over, and both talks got better for every round. It worked. But the next talk always began with a copy of the last one, and the rules drifted a little each time. A fix stayed in the talk where I made it. So I put the method in one place. You're looking at it.

content.heading: Write the talk first
content.lead: Your assistant writes the whole talk into one file. The deck and storyboard are built from it.

items.label: files to present and practice with

content.footer: This deck was built the same way.

notes.say: Write the talk first. Your assistant keeps the whole talk in one file, every slide with its timing and the words you'll say. The sources behind the facts go in there too. It checks that file before anything gets built. Then it builds two things from it: the deck you present and a storyboard to practice with. Both open in any browser. You can mail them or open them on a plane. If something needs to change, you just say so, and the assistant changes the file and builds both again. Nobody touches a slide by hand, so the slides never drift from the script. This deck was built exactly that way.

items.title: Checks
items.text: Broken timing caught before the build

items.title: Deck
items.text: Keyboard control and a rehearse mode

notes.do: Walk the cards left to right.
notes.say: There are four parts, and the checks come first. Before anything is built, the assistant checks the talk and stops if a slide appears twice or the minutes don't add up. An em dash will stop it too. (Yes, the em dash. I have opinions.) The deck runs in any browser and works from the keyboard. There's a rehearse mode I'll show you. Then you've got the storyboard, with every slide and the full script alongside a running clock for practice. The stage templates are where you do the thinking: a file for each stage, before you make slides.

items.title: Use it when
items.text: The talk matters and you want the thinking done before the slides.

items.title: Skip it when
items.text: A one-page update would do. Write the page.

notes.do: Be honest. Name when to skip it.
notes.say: If you give talks, this is for you. Keynotes and workshops, customer sessions, that all-hands where you've got twelve minutes and far too much to say. When the talk matters, the preparation pays back. But please don't do all this for a weekly status update. You don't need a voice prompt and a counterargument to tell people what happened this week. Write a page and send it. I mean that. And if the talk is tomorrow and you've only got one evening, go straight to the outline and rehearsal, because those two stages will help you most.

content.heading: Six stages
content.lead: From idea to rehearsal. Outline and Deck are loops.

notes.do: Trace the top row, then the bottom row. Stop on Outline and Deck.
notes.say: Six stages. The first two are about finding the thought: you talk about the idea, and the research checks it. The other four shape the talk. You plan the minutes, write the outline, build the deck and rehearse it. Each stage leaves a file behind, with a gate that tells you when you've done enough to move on. Outline and Deck are loops, though. You'll go through them many times, and most of your rounds happen there. That's fine. The rounds are the work.

items.title: Talk about the idea
items.text: Out loud and unedited. Not the whole talk.

items.title: Say who it's for
items.text: In the same take: the audience, the event, your minutes

notes.do: Spend the time on the voice prompt.
notes.say: It starts with you talking. Five or ten minutes, out loud, about the idea. Not the whole talk, nobody's asking for chapters yet. Just the thought you want to test and why it matters to you. In the same take you say who'll be in the room, what kind of event it is and how many minutes you've got. I just dictate in Copilot CLI. The assistant keeps the transcript word for word and pulls out the claims to check, but it doesn't get to improve what I said. Then comes the research: the facts and the strongest counterargument for every claim, plus your own old decks and notes. You've probably said half of this before. Maybe better than you remember.

items.title: Planning
items.text: Goal, chapters and minutes that add up

items.title: Outline
items.text: The full script, round after round

items.title: Deck
items.text: Built from the outline, slide by slide

items.title: Rehearsal
items.text: Against the clock, until it sticks

notes.say: Planning starts from what you said about the room. What should people do afterwards? How many minutes do you really have? Split them into chapters, and the assistant checks that they add up. Then write the whole talk as an outline, with timing and a script for every slide, and keep rewriting it until it works. The deck is built from that. You'll polish it slide by slide, then practice against the clock until two runs in a row fit inside the slot. And when the deck looks done, you'll want to stop. Keep going.

content.heading: Most rounds happen before the deck
content.footer: One keynote I prepared this autumn.

notes.say: Real numbers, from one keynote I prepared this autumn. Thirty minutes on stage. Behind them: fourteen versions of the outline and three drafts of the deck. Look at the ratio. Most of the work happened before I had slides to look at, and that's where the assistant helped me most. By round fourteen, rebuilding the practice flow took a minute. By hand it would have taken an evening. So when you plan your preparation, put the time there. A deck draft is cheap. A clear outline is not.

sources.label: Author's preparation log for one 30-minute keynote, November 2026

data.text: Never rewrite the presenter's idea or voice prompt.

notes.say: The assistant never rewrites your idea or your voice prompt. That's the rule I care about most. It can ask questions and do the research, then build and check the result. It can tell you a claim is weak. But you decide what you believe and choose the final words, because you have to believe every sentence when you stand up there. Somebody else polishing a sentence for you won't make you believe it. I've tried. It shows on stage.

content.heading: Bring your own assistant
content.lead: Copilot Cowork, GitHub Copilot CLI or GitHub Copilot in VS Code. Use the one you already have.

data.text: Add the skill once. It runs the stages with you and stops at every gate for your call.

notes.do: Name the assistant you use. Don't install anything live.
notes.say: You don't run any of this by hand. You add one skill to the assistant you already use, and you only do that once. In Cowork you upload it. In Copilot CLI or VS Code you ask Copilot to install it from the repository. After that it's a conversation. The assistant works out where your talk stands and runs the next stage with you, and at every gate it stops and asks before it goes on. I use Copilot CLI myself. The skill is the same everywhere.

content.heading: Your first deck
content.lead: Four steps, all in the conversation with your assistant.

items: Add the Slidemaster skill to your assistant
Say: help me prepare my next talk
Talk about your idea, then answer its questions
Open the deck and the storyboard it builds

notes.do: Read the second step the way you'd say it to your assistant.
notes.say: Four steps, and all of them happen in the conversation. Add the skill. Then say: help me prepare my next talk. The assistant asks you to talk about the idea and who it's for. After that you answer one question at a time, in your own words. When you've approved the outline, it builds the deck and the storyboard and checks every slide before you see them. Then you open them in your browser and start rehearsing.

content.heading: Rehearse against the clock
content.lead: Your assistant compares every run with your plan.

steps: Start a timed run from the storyboard
Hand the run to your assistant

notes.do: Point out that only you see the timer.
notes.say: Rehearsal is the stage everyone skips. Let me show you what you'd be skipping. Open the storyboard and select Start a timed run, and the deck gets a small timer that only you can see. Present the whole talk out loud. On the last slide you save the run and hand it to your assistant, and it compares every chapter and every slide with your plan. Now you've got something concrete when you decide where to cut. Then do it again. Two runs in a row inside the slot, and you're done.

items: Talk about the idea for five minutes, unedited
Say who it's for and what kind of event it is
Let your assistant take it from there, with the skill

notes.do: End on the first action. Leave the slide up.
notes.say: So here's my ask. Before you open a single slide for your next talk, talk about the idea. Five minutes, out loud and unedited. Not the whole talk, just the thought you want to test. And while you're at it, say who'll be in the room and what kind of event it is. Do it straight into your assistant, with the skill added. Then let it take over. The repository is open and MIT licensed, so take what works for you. And if you build something better, tell me. Thanks.
